title: SQL and data modelling for CTOs
objectives: Design relational schemas that fit the workload

sources.title: PostgreSQL documentation
sources.reviewDepth: Official documentation reviewed at overview level.

verificationNotes: SQL dialects differ; verify syntax and features against your database.

sections.heading: Relational modelling
sections.body: Model entities and relationships with normalised tables, clear primary keys and foreign keys. Normalise to reduce anomalies, then denormalise deliberately for read performance. Name columns consistently and avoid encoding multiple facts in one field.

sections.heading: Writing SQL
sections.body: Use explicit joins, filter early, and aggregate with care. Understand NULL semantics, transaction isolation and locking. Prefer set-based operations over row-by-row processing. Explain query plans before optimising.

sections.heading: Performance
sections.body: Index the columns used in filters and joins, but not everything. Watch for full table scans, N+1 queries and missing pagination. Measure with EXPLAIN and real data volumes. Cache hot reads where appropriate.

sections.heading: Migrations and data quality
sections.body: Use versioned migrations that are reversible where possible. Back up before risky changes. Add constraints, checks and not-null rules to protect data quality. Test migrations against production-like data. Keep destructive changes separate from additive ones.

sections.heading: SQL versus NoSQL
sections.body: SQL suits relational data, complex queries and strong consistency. NoSQL suits flexible schemas, massive scale and simple access patterns. The choice should follow access patterns and consistency needs, not fashion.

workedExample.title: School data model (illustrative)
workedExample.body: Tables: schools, students, enrolments, attendance. Foreign keys link enrolments to students and schools. An index on attendance(student_id, date) supports reporting. A migration adds a not-null constraint after backfilling data.
